title: Measuring retrieval: recall@k, MRR, nDCG

kcs.statement: Retrieval quality is measured on labelled queries.
Compute recall@k and precision@k for a ranked list.
Compute MRR; nDCG weights graded relevance by rank.

visual_fit.why: Recall and precision change as k grows; a chart of the worked example shows both curves at once.

glossary.md: Of all relevant items, the fraction found in the top k.
The mean over queries of 1 / (rank of the first relevant result).

md: “It looks good on three queries I tried” is not an evaluation. To **measure** retrieval you need a **labelled set**: queries, each with the chunks that are truly relevant. Sources, from best to worst: real user queries labelled by people, queries written by domain experts, and LLM-generated queries that a human has checked.
Then score the retriever's top-k list for each query:

- [[recall@k]]: of the relevant chunks, what fraction appear in the top k? This is the main metric when an LLM will read the top k (RAG).
- **precision@k**: of the top k, what fraction are relevant?
- [[MRR]] (mean reciprocal rank): 1 / (rank of the first relevant result), averaged over queries. It rewards putting a right answer *first*.
- **nDCG**: rewards relevant results near the top and supports graded relevance (very relevant vs somewhat relevant).

block.title: Score one query
block.problem_md: Relevant chunks for a query: **{D2, D7}**. The retriever returns **[D5, D2, D9, D1, D7]**.

steps.md: recall@3: the top 3 are D5, D2, D9. Only D2 is relevant, so 1 of 2 = **0.5**
recall@5: D2 and D7 are both in the top 5, so 2 of 2 = **1.0**
Reciprocal rank: the first relevant result (D2) is at rank 2, so RR = **1/2**
steps.why_md: Average RR over all queries to get MRR.

block.answer_md: recall@3 = 0.5, recall@5 = 1.0, RR = 0.5. Here k matters a lot: if your LLM only reads 3 chunks, it never sees D7.

block.explain_md: If a query has no relevant result in the list, its reciprocal rank is 0.

parts.means: how many chunks are truly relevant
position of the first relevant result for query q

question.prompt_md: Relevant: **{A, B, C}**. Top-5 returned: **[X, A, Y, C, Z]**. What is recall@5? (2 decimals)

common_wrong.why_md: 0.4 is precision@5 (2 relevant out of 5 returned). Recall divides by the 3 relevant chunks.

question.solution_md: Found A and C: 2 of the 3 relevant. 2/3 ≈ 0.67.

question.prompt_md: Over 3 queries, the first relevant result appears at rank **1**, rank **3**, and **not at all**. What is the MRR? (2 decimals)

common_wrong.why_md: You dropped the query with no relevant result. It contributes 0 and still counts in the average.

block.title: One query: recall@k and precision@k as k grows
block.alt: A bar chart for the worked example, relevant chunks D2 and D7 in the list D5, D2, D9, D1, D7. Recall@k is 0, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5 and 1.0 for k from 1 to 5. Precision@k is 0, 0.5, 0.33, 0.25 and 0.4.
block.caption_md: Recall only rises when a relevant chunk appears (D2 at rank 2, D7 at rank 5); precision falls with every miss.

recap.formula: recall@k = relevant in top-k ÷ all relevant · MRR = mean of 1 ÷ rank of the first relevant hit
recap.pitfall: recall@k says nothing about where in the top-k the hit sits; MRR does.

anticipated_doubts.question: Recall vs precision: which matters for search?
anticipated_doubts.answer_md: **Recall@k** asks: of everything relevant, how much did we surface in the top k? **Precision@k** asks: of the top k, how much is relevant? For RAG, recall usually matters most (the LLM can ignore junk, but it can't use what it never saw). For a results page people read, precision near the top (MRR, nDCG) matters more.
anticipated_doubts.deeper_md: Fishing with a net. Recall: what fraction of the fish in the lake did you catch? Precision: what fraction of your catch is fish rather than boots? A huge net catches all the fish and lots of boots (high recall, low precision).

bridge.title: Same results, two metrics
md: Relevant: {A, B}. Top-5 returned: [A, X, Y, Z, B].

- recall@5 = 2/2 = **1.0**: found everything.
- precision@5 = 2/5 = **0.4**: most results are junk.
- MRR = 1/1 = **1.0**: the first result is relevant.
An LLM reading 5 chunks is fine here. A human scanning a results page wastes three looks.

verify.prompt_md: Relevant {A}. Top-4 [X, Y, A, Z]. Precision@4?
